author.name: Alfred J. Church
author.biography: A schoolmaster who became professor of Latin at University College London, he retold many Greek and Roman stories for young readers.

hook.text: What would it take to get home after twenty years away, with strangers feasting in your hall?

paragraphs: Troy has fallen and the Greek chiefs have sailed for home, but Ulysses, the cleverest of them, has still not come home almost ten years later. The goddess Calypso keeps him on her island. On Ithaca, princes from the islands court his wife Penelope, claiming he is dead, and feast on his flocks and wine while his son Telemachus watches. The goddess Athene decides it is time for both father and son to act.

The book begins with the son. Telemachus sails to Pylos and Sparta to ask his father's old comrades for news. Then it turns to Ulysses himself: freed from Calypso, wrecked on his raft and washed ashore among the Phaeacians, he tells their king the story of his wanderings, from the Cyclops and the enchantress Circe to the land of the dead, the Sirens, Scylla and the cattle of the Sun.
The second half takes place on Ithaca. Ulysses comes home looking like an old beggar, and the story turns on who will know him, whom he can trust and how long he can wait.
Alfred Church retold Homer's Odyssey for young readers in plain prose. It is not a translation of the Greek poem, but it follows Homer's story in Homer's order, with the gods taking part throughout.

orientation.text: Twenty-five short chapters, beginning with an introduction to the Greek world and its gods. The text calls the hero Ulysses, the Latin form of Odysseus, and numbered notes at the end of each chapter show how to say the Greek names.
